beijing.metaTitle: Beijing Travel Guide — Where History Meets Modernity | CN Rover
beijing.metaDesc: Complete Beijing travel guide: Great Wall, Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, best time to visit, transportation tips, and curated itineraries.
beijing.heroSubtitle: A capital shaped by 3,000 years of history. From the majestic Great Wall to the sprawling Forbidden City, from lively hutongs to cutting-edge art districts — Beijing is a city that captivates every traveler.
beijing.overviewText: Beijing (Běijīng), meaning "Northern Capital," is the capital of China and a globally renowned historical and cultural city. With over 3,000 years of history and 800 years as an imperial capital, it boasts 7 UNESCO World Heritage Sites — more than any other city in the world. Today, Beijing is a dynamic metropolis where ancient grandeur meets modern innovation.
beijing.transportHubText:
Beijing has two international airports (Capital International PEK and Daxing International PKX), plus Asia's largest high-speed rail hub, Beijing South Station.

Getting around: The Beijing metro has 27 lines covering the entire city, with fares from 3-9 RMB. Use Alipay's transit code or download the "Beijing Yikatong" app.
beijing.topAttractionsText: Beijing has so much to explore. Here are the highlights:
beijing.foodPekingDuckDesc: Beijing's most famous dish — crispy skin, tender meat. Try Quanjude (oldest, most famous) or Sijimin Fu (preferred by locals).
beijing.foodZhajiangmianDesc: Beijing's signature noodle dish: thick wheat noodles topped with a savory fermented soybean paste and fresh vegetables.
beijing.foodDumplingsDesc: Traditional northern Chinese dumplings with various fillings. Try Jin Ding Xuan or Din Tai Fung.
beijing.foodHotpotDesc: Traditional copper-pot hotpot with thinly sliced lamb, dipped in sesame sauce — a Beijing winter staple. Try Donglaishun.
beijing.tip1Desc: Popular attractions like the Forbidden City and Great Wall require advance booking through WeChat mini-programs or official websites. Book at least a week ahead during peak season.
beijing.tip2Desc: WeChat, Alipay, Amap (navigation), and Didi (ride-hailing) are essential. Download and set them up before you arrive.
beijing.tip3Desc: Air pollution can be an issue in autumn and winter. Check the AQI before heading out and carry a mask if needed.
beijing.tip4Desc: Buy a "Beijing Municipal Transportation Card" at any metro station, or simply use Alipay/WeChat to scan and ride the subway and buses.

greatWall.metaTitle: Great Wall Guide — Which Section Should You Visit? | CN Rover
greatWall.metaDesc: Complete Great Wall travel guide: Badaling vs Mutianyu vs Simatai vs Jinshanling — how to get there, ticket prices, best time to visit, and practical tips.
greatWall.heroSubtitle: You haven't truly been to China until you've climbed the Great Wall. This UNESCO World Heritage site spans over 21,000 km and is China's most iconic landmark.
greatWall.intro: The Great Wall (Chángchéng) is one of the most remarkable architectural achievements in human history. Construction began as early as the 7th century BC, and the wall stretches over 21,000 kilometers across northern China. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Several sections near Beijing are open to visitors, each with its own character.
greatWall.whichSectionIntro: Several sections of the Great Wall near Beijing are open to tourists. Here's how to choose:
greatWall.badalingDesc: The most famous and busiest section. Well-restored with cable cars and full facilities. Best for first-time visitors, families, and those short on time.
greatWall.badalingHowToGet: Getting there: Take the high-speed train from Beijing North Station to Badaling (25 min), or bus 877 from Deshengmen.
greatWall.badalingTicket: Tickets: ¥40 peak season, ¥35 off-peak. Cable car round-trip ¥140.
greatWall.mutianyuDesc: The favorite section among international visitors. Less crowded than Badaling with spectacular scenery. Features a toboggan slide for the descent. Excellent English signage.
greatWall.mutianyuHowToGet: Getting there: Take bus 916 Express from Dongzhimen to Huairou, then transfer to bus H23 or a taxi. Direct tourist buses are also available.
greatWall.mutianyuTicket: Tickets: ¥45. Cable car round-trip ¥140, toboggan slide ¥100.
greatWall.simataiDesc: Known for its steep, rugged terrain and original Ming Dynasty appearance. Adjacent to Gubei Water Town — visit the town by day and night-climb the wall. Great for photographers and adventurers.
greatWall.simataiHowToGet: Getting there: Take the direct tourist bus from Dongzhimen to Gubei Water Town (~2 hrs). Self-driving is also convenient.
greatWall.simataiTicket: Tickets: Simatai ¥40, Gubei Water Town ¥140. Night climbing requires a separate ticket.
greatWall.jinshanlingDesc: The most photographer-friendly section. The wall snakes along mountain ridges with sweeping views and very few tourists. Ideal for hikers and serious photographers.
greatWall.jinshanlingHowToGet: Getting there: Take the bus to Luanping from Wangjing West Station and get off at Jinshanling. Self-driving or a private car is recommended.
greatWall.tip1: Wear comfortable hiking shoes — the steps are uneven and steep in places.
greatWall.tip2: Bring plenty of water and snacks. Prices on the wall are high.
greatWall.tip3: Avoid Chinese public holidays (May 1st, October 1st, Chinese New Year) — the crowds are enormous.
greatWall.tip4: Sunscreen on sunny days, a jacket on overcast days. It's always windy at the top.
greatWall.tip5: Go early in the morning — afternoon light is better for photos, but morning means smaller crowds.
greatWall.tip6: Some sections are very steep. Take the cable car if you have knee problems.

forbiddenCity.metaTitle: Forbidden City Guide — Complete Visit Guide | CN Rover
forbiddenCity.metaDesc: Complete guide to visiting the Forbidden City (Palace Museum): ticket booking, recommended routes, must-see highlights, and practical tips.
forbiddenCity.heroSubtitle: The world's largest ancient palace complex — 500 years of imperial history, now China's most treasured cultural heritage site.
forbiddenCity.intro: The Forbidden City (Gùgōng / Zǐjìnchéng) was the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing dynasties for over 500 years. Located at the center of Beijing's central axis, it covers 720,000 square meters with more than 9,000 rooms. It is the largest collection of ancient wooden structures in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
forbiddenCity.bookingText:
Tickets must be booked in advance through the official "Palace Museum" WeChat mini-program or the official website (https://www.dpm.org.cn). During peak season, book at least 7-10 days ahead.

Ticket prices: Peak season ¥60, off-peak ¥40. The Treasure Gallery and Clock & Watch Gallery each cost an additional ¥10.

Opening hours: Tuesday–Sunday 8:30–17:00 (peak) / 16:30 (off-peak). Closed on Mondays.
forbiddenCity.routeOptions: We've designed three routes for different time budgets:
forbiddenCity.route2hDesc: Meridian Gate → Hall of Supreme Harmony → Hall of Central Harmony → Hall of Preserving Harmony → Palace of Heavenly Purity → Gate of Divine Might. Just the central axis — the essential halls.
forbiddenCity.route4hDesc: Meridian Gate → Hall of Supreme Harmony → Hall of Central Harmony → Hall of Preserving Harmony → Palace of Heavenly Purity → Palace of Earthly Tranquility → Imperial Garden → Western Six Palaces (Empress Dowager's residence) → Treasure Gallery → Gate of Divine Might.
forbiddenCity.routeFullDesc: Meridian Gate → Hall of Martial Valor (calligraphy gallery) → Hall of Supreme Harmony → Hall of Central Harmony → Hall of Preserving Harmony → Palace of Heavenly Purity → Palace of Earthly Tranquility → Imperial Garden → Eastern Six Palaces (including Treasure Gallery and Clock Gallery) → Hall of Ancestral Worship (Clock Gallery) → Gate of Divine Might.
forbiddenCity.highlight1Desc: The largest and most important hall in the Forbidden City, used for the emperor's coronation and major ceremonies. The bronze lions, cranes, and turtles in front are masterpieces.
forbiddenCity.highlight2Desc: The sleeping quarters of 14 Ming emperors and two early Qing emperors (Shunzhi and Kangxi). Famous for its "Upright and Brilliant" plaque.
forbiddenCity.highlight3Desc: A stunning collection of imperial jewelry, gold, jade, and porcelain. Highlights include the Empress Dowager's phoenix crown.
forbiddenCity.highlight4Desc: The royal garden at the north end of the Forbidden City, with ancient trees, pavilions, and rockeries — a great spot for photos.
forbiddenCity.tip1: Enter with your passport (original, not a photo). Foreigners CANNOT use ID card scanning.
forbiddenCity.tip2: Audio guides (¥40) are available at the entrance with English narration.
forbiddenCity.tip3: Bring your own water and snacks — options inside are limited and expensive.
forbiddenCity.tip4: Wear comfortable shoes. The Forbidden City is enormous and you'll be walking all day.
forbiddenCity.tip5: Enter from the south gate (Meridian Gate) and exit from the north gate (Gate of Divine Might). Walk across to Jingshan Park for a panoramic view of the entire complex.

itineraries.metaTitle: Beijing Itineraries — 3-Day and 5-Day Perfect Routes | CN Rover
itineraries.metaDesc: Beijing travel itineraries: 3-day highlights route and 5-day in-depth route, including the Great Wall, Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, hutongs, and local food.
itineraries.heroSubtitle: Whether you have 3 days or 5, we've designed the perfect routes to make the most of your time in Beijing.
itineraries.day1Am: Morning: Forbidden City (at least 3 hrs) → Jingshan Park (panoramic view of the Forbidden City)
itineraries.day1Pm: Afternoon: Beihai Park → Shichahai → Yandai Xiejie (hutong exploration)
itineraries.day1Evening: Evening: Nanluoguxiang (street food and boutique shops)
itineraries.day1Note: Arrive early — enter the Forbidden City right when it opens to beat the crowds.
itineraries.day2Am: Morning: Head to Mutianyu Great Wall (recommended — fewer crowds)
itineraries.day2Pm: Afternoon: Continue exploring the wall → return to the city
itineraries.day2Evening: Evening: Peking Duck dinner (Sijimin Fu recommended)
itineraries.day2Note: The Great Wall is far from the city center. Leave before 8am.
itineraries.day3Title: Day 3: Temple of Heaven & Hutong Culture
itineraries.day3Am: Morning: Temple of Heaven (Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, Echo Wall)
itineraries.day3Pm: Afternoon: Qianmen Street → Dashilan → Yangmeizhu Xiejie (old Beijing shopping district)
itineraries.day3Evening: Evening: Wangfujing Street (shopping and street food)
itineraries.day3Note: Buy a combo ticket for the Temple of Heaven to enter the main buildings.
itineraries.day4Pm: Afternoon: Summer Palace (royal garden, at least 3 hrs)
itineraries.day4Evening: Evening: Ghost Street / Guijie (spicy crayfish and late-night eats)
itineraries.day4Note: The 798 Art District is very photogenic — spend a relaxed morning wandering. Visit the Summer Palace in the afternoon for sunset over Kunming Lake.
itineraries.day5Am: Morning: Yonghe Temple (Lama Temple, Tibetan Buddhist) → Confucius Temple & Imperial College
itineraries.day5Pm: Afternoon: Sanlitun or Solana (shopping and leisure)
itineraries.day5Evening: Pack up and prepare for departure
itineraries.summaryDay1: Day 1: Imperial Central Axis (Forbidden City, Jingshan, Shichahai)
itineraries.summaryDay3: Day 3: Temple of Heaven & Old Beijing
itineraries.recommendation: If you only have 3 days, do Day 1 + Day 2 + Day 3. With 5 days, you can do it all. If you have extra time, take a relaxed morning wandering the 798 Art District — Beijing's creative heart.

visaGuide.metaTitle: China Visa Guide — Types, Application, and Visa-Free Policies | CN Rover
visaGuide.metaDesc: Complete China visa guide: tourist visa (L visa) application process, required documents, visa-free policies, and 144-hour transit without visa.
visaGuide.heroSubtitle: Understanding China's visa system — types, how to apply, and the latest visa-free policies.
visaGuide.typeLDesc: The most common visa type for tourists visiting China. Usually valid for 30 days, single or multiple entry.
visaGuide.typeMDesc: For foreign nationals traveling to China for business activities.
visaGuide.typeXDesc: For foreign nationals studying in China.
visaGuide.step1: Fill out the online visa application form (on the China Visa Application Service Center website)
visaGuide.step2: Book an appointment and submit documents in person at the visa center
visaGuide.step3: Submit your passport, photo, flight and hotel bookings, etc.
visaGuide.step4: Pay the fee and wait for processing (usually 4-5 business days)
visaGuide.doc1: Passport valid for at least 6 months
visaGuide.visaFreeText:
China currently has visa-free agreements with several countries including France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Malaysia, Singapore, and others. Visa-free stays are typically up to 15 days.

Always check the latest visa-free policy before departing, as policies are updated frequently.
visaGuide.transitText:
Citizens of 54 countries (including the US, Canada, UK, Australia, and others) can enjoy 144 hours (6 days) of visa-free transit in cities like Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou.

Requirements: Hold a valid flight ticket to a third country and any required visas. Stay within the designated city/region for no more than 144 hours.
visaGuide.tip1: Visa policies change frequently. Check with the Chinese embassy in your country for the latest information before traveling.
visaGuide.tip2: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months.
visaGuide.tip3: Apply for your visa 1-2 months before your trip.
visaGuide.tip4: Register your accommodation with local police within 24 hours of arrival (hotels handle this automatically).

paymentGuide.metaTitle: China Payment Guide — Alipay & WeChat Pay for Foreigners | CN Rover
paymentGuide.metaDesc: How to use mobile payments in China as a foreign tourist: setting up Alipay and WeChat Pay with international credit cards, and cash tips.
paymentGuide.heroSubtitle: China runs on mobile payments. Setting up Alipay and WeChat Pay will make your trip infinitely smoother.
paymentGuide.alipayDesc: Alipay is China's largest mobile payment platform. It now supports international credit card binding (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) and offers a Tour Pass feature.
paymentGuide.alipayStep1: Download the Alipay app and register with your overseas phone number
paymentGuide.alipayStep2: Select "International" mode and bind your international credit card
paymentGuide.alipayStep3: Optional: Top up via Tour Pass
paymentGuide.alipayStep4: Scan to pay — show your payment code at stores, or scan the merchant's QR code
paymentGuide.wechatDesc: WeChat Pay is integrated into the WeChat messaging app — China's other dominant payment platform.
paymentGuide.wechatStep1: Download WeChat and register with your overseas phone number
paymentGuide.wechatStep2: Go to "Me" → "Services" and activate WeChat Pay
paymentGuide.wechatStep3: Bind an international credit card (coverage varies by card issuer)
paymentGuide.wechatStep4: Send red packets and transfer money to friends
paymentGuide.cashDesc:
While mobile payments dominate, carrying some cash is always a good idea:

- ATMs at airports and banks accept international cards for RMB withdrawals
- Keep ¥200–500 in cash for emergencies
- Some small vendors and taxis only accept cash or QR code payments
- ¥100, ¥50, ¥20, and ¥10 notes are most practical
paymentGuide.tip1: Download Alipay and WeChat from your local App Store BEFORE arriving in China — the Chinese App Store may be inaccessible.
paymentGuide.tip2: International credit card transactions may incur cross-border fees from your bank.
paymentGuide.tip3: Always carry some small bills for street food, small shops, and some taxis.
paymentGuide.tip4: Large malls, hotels, and chain restaurants accept international credit cards, but small shops overwhelmingly use WeChat/Alipay.

simGuide.metaTitle: China SIM Card & Internet Guide — How to Stay Connected | CN Rover
simGuide.metaDesc: How to get internet in China: buy a local SIM card, use eSIM, choose international roaming, and VPN tips for accessing blocked websites.
simGuide.heroSubtitle: How to stay connected in China — from SIM cards to eSIMs, from roaming to VPNs.
simGuide.option1Desc:
Buy a temporary SIM card at the airport or a carrier store after arriving in China. Three major carriers: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom.

China Mobile has the best coverage. Airports offer special foreigner plans (7/15/30 days) with data and calls. Price: ~¥100–300.

You need your passport to purchase.
simGuide.option2Desc:
Install an eSIM on your phone before departure — it activates as soon as you land in China. Recommended services:

- Airalo: Multiple China data plans, easy setup
- Nomad eSIM: Competitive pricing
- Holafly: Unlimited data plans

The advantage: no need to swap your physical SIM, you keep your home number. The downside: data only (no voice calls).
simGuide.option3Desc:
Activate international roaming on your existing phone plan and use your home number in China.

The advantage: simple and no SIM swapping needed. The downside: more expensive, and some sites (Google, etc.) may still be inaccessible.
simGuide.vpnDesc:
China's internet landscape is different — Google, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and many other sites are not directly accessible.

If you need to access these services while in China:

1. Install a VPN app and subscribe before leaving home
2. Recommended: ExpressVPN, NordVPN, Astrill — these still work in China
3. IMPORTANT: Install BEFORE arriving in China, as you won't be able to download them here

⚠️ Important: VPN policies may change. Check the latest information before your trip.
simGuide.rec1: Quickest option: Buy an Airalo eSIM before departure, keep your home SIM for SMS/verification codes
simGuide.rec2: Most reliable: Buy a China Mobile foreigner SIM at the airport — best coverage
simGuide.rec3: Best combo: eSIM for data + international roaming to keep your home number active

transportGuide.metaTitle: China Transportation Guide — High-Speed Rail, Metro, Taxis | CN Rover
transportGuide.metaDesc: How to get around China: high-speed rail booking, metro systems, taxis and ride-hailing with Didi, and shared bikes.
transportGuide.heroSubtitle: China has the world's most extensive high-speed rail network and incredibly efficient urban transit systems. Here's how to use them.
transportGuide.highSpeedRailDesc:
China's high-speed rail network covers over 42,000 km, connecting every major city.

- Beijing to Shanghai: as fast as 4.5 hours
- Beijing to Xi'an: about 4 hours
- Beijing to Chengdu: about 7.5 hours

How to buy tickets:
- Use the "Railway 12306" app (supports passport registration)
- Buy at station counters or self-service machines
- Book via Trip.com international version (small service fee)

Seat classes: Second class (budget-friendly), First class (more legroom), Business class (fully reclining seats).
transportGuide.subwayDesc:
All major Chinese cities have modern metro systems.

- Beijing: 27 lines, ¥3–9 per ride
- Shanghai: 20 lines, ¥3–15 per ride
- Chengdu: 13 lines, ¥2–10 per ride

How to ride:
1. Buy a ticket at the station (cash or QR payment)
2. Use Alipay/WeChat transit code to scan in/out
3. Buy a transit card (many cities accept the same nationwide card)

Metro hours are typically 5:30am–11:00pm.
transportGuide.taxiDesc:
Two ways to get a ride in China:

1. Taxis: Flag down a passing cab on the street (flagfall ~¥13). Have your destination written in Chinese or show your phone with navigation.

2. Ride-hailing: Use Didi Chuxing (DiDi), China's largest ride-hailing platform.
- Download the Didi app and register with your overseas phone number
- Supports international credit cards
- Options: Express, Premier, Hitch, etc.
- You can also access Didi through Alipay

Note: Uber no longer operates in China. Didi is the replacement.
transportGuide.bikeDesc:
Shared bikes are everywhere in Chinese cities — perfect for short trips.

- Major brands: Meituan Bike, HelloBike, Qingju
- How to ride: Scan the QR code with Alipay or WeChat
- Cost: ~¥1–1.5 per 30 minutes
- Park only in designated areas
transportGuide.appDesc:
Transportation apps you need:
- Amap (高德地图) or Baidu Maps: navigation and route planning (more accurate than Google Maps in China)
- Railway 12306: high-speed rail tickets
- Didi: ride-hailing
- Meituan or Dianping: restaurant and attraction reviews

faq.metaTitle: FAQ — China Travel Frequently Asked Questions | CN Rover
faq.metaDesc: Common questions about traveling in China: visa, payments, language, safety, and more.
faq.pageSubtitle: Common questions travelers have about visiting China.
faq.q1: Can I travel in Beijing without speaking Chinese?
faq.a1: Yes, absolutely. Beijing is a very international city — airports, major attractions, large malls, and hotels all have English signage and staff. Still, we recommend: 1) Download a translation app (Google Translate or Pleco); 2) Learn a few basic phrases like "xiè xie" (thank you) and "duō shao qián" (how much); 3) Use navigation apps with Chinese addresses for better accuracy.
faq.q2: Can I use Google Maps in China?
faq.a2: Google Maps does not work properly in China. Use Amap (高德地图) or Baidu Maps instead. Amap has an English interface. Both are far more accurate than Google Maps for navigation and public transit in China.
faq.q3: Do I need a VPN in China?
faq.a3: If you need access to Google, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, or similar services, yes. Install a VPN app and subscribe to a service BEFORE arriving in China, as you won't be able to download it once you're here.
faq.a4: China is one of the safest countries in the world, with a very low crime rate. Even walking alone late at night in major cities is generally safe. Just use common sense and keep an eye on your belongings.
faq.q5: Can I use international credit cards?
faq.a5: Large malls, brand hotels, and chain restaurants accept international credit cards (Visa, Mastercard, etc.). However, small shops, restaurants, taxis, and street vendors overwhelmingly use WeChat/Alipay or cash. We recommend linking Alipay or WeChat Pay to your international card.
faq.q6: Can I drink tap water in China?
faq.a6: Tap water is not drinkable in China. Drink bottled or boiled water. Hotels provide complimentary bottled water daily. Convenience stores are everywhere — a 500ml bottle costs about ¥2.
faq.q7: What kind of power plugs does China use?
faq.a7: China uses Type A (two flat pins) and Type I (three flat pins) sockets. Voltage is 220V at 50Hz. Bring a universal travel adapter.
faq.a8: China has no tipping culture. Tipping is not expected anywhere. High-end restaurants may add a 10-15% service charge, but standard restaurants and taxis do not expect tips. Feel free to tip or not — it won't affect service.

about.heroSubtitle: Helping every international visitor discover China with confidence.
about.storyText:
CN Rover was created by a group of travel enthusiasts in China. We noticed that while more and more international visitors are coming to China, high-quality English travel information is still scarce.

Many English guides are outdated, and visitors often struggle with payments, internet access, transportation, and other practical challenges upon arrival.

Our mission is to bridge that gap — providing current, practical, and trustworthy travel information to help every international visitor have a better experience in China.
about.mission1: Provide the most up-to-date and accurate China travel information
about.mission2: Bridge the gap between Chinese and English travel resources
about.mission3: Help international visitors discover a real, diverse, and welcoming China
